title: Code Review Expert
description: Get a senior engineer-level code review on any code snippet.
content: You are a senior software engineer conducting a thorough code review. Analyze the following code for: 1) Correctness and edge cases 2) Performance bottlenecks 3) Security vulnerabilities 4) Maintainability and readability 5) Design patterns and best practices. Provide specific, actionable feedback with examples. Code to review: {code}

title: Debug Like a Detective
description: Systematic debugging methodology for any error.
content: You are debugging the following error. Walk through a systematic investigation: 1) State what you know from the error message 2) List your top 3 hypotheses 3) For each hypothesis, describe how you would test it 4) Identify the most likely root cause 5) Propose a fix and explain why it works. Error: {error_message}. Context: {context}

title: SQL Query Optimizer
description: Turn slow SQL queries into fast ones with expert analysis. Output: Optimized SQL query in text.
content: Analyze this SQL query for performance issues. Identify: 1) Missing indexes 2) Inefficient joins 3) N+1 query patterns 4) Unnecessary subqueries 5) Column selection issues. Rewrite the query for optimal performance and explain each change. Query: {sql_query}

title: The Ruthless Editor
description: A no-mercy edit that strips fat and leaves only signal. Output: Edited text with markup.
content: You are a world-class editor known for brutal honesty. Review the following text and: 1) Identify every word that earns zero weight — cut it 2) Flag passive voice and rewrite it active 3) Mark clichés and replace with specifics 4) Rate each paragraph for signal-to-noise ratio 5) Rewrite the weakest paragraph as a model. Be merciless. Good writing has no room for sentiment. Text: {text}

title: Cold Email that Converts
description: High-converting cold emails with zero fluff. Output: Ready-to-send email copy.
content: Write a cold outreach email for {product/service} targeting {target_persona}. Requirements: 1) Subject line under 8 words with a specific hook 2) Opening line references something real about their company 3) Problem statement in one sentence 4) Value proposition with a measurable claim 5) Single CTA that takes under 2 minutes to act on. No buzzwords. No "I hope this email finds you well."

title: Brand Voice Architect
description: Build a distinctive brand voice that stands apart from the noise. Output: Brand voice guide in text.
content: Define a comprehensive brand voice for {company_name} in {industry}. Deliver: 1) Three words that capture the personality (with anti-examples for each) 2) How this voice differs from the top 3 competitors 3) Writing examples in this voice vs. generic voice 4) 10 words this brand says / 10 words it never says 5) A paragraph in this voice about the company mission. Target audience: {audience}.

title: UX Heuristic Audit
description: Rigorous heuristic evaluation with actionable improvements. Output: Heuristic audit report in text.
content: Conduct a UX audit of the following interface description using Nielsen's 10 heuristics. For each heuristic: 1) Score it 1-10 2) Identify the specific violation if any 3) Provide a concrete improvement recommendation. Then rank the top 3 issues by impact on user success. Interface: {interface_description}

title: Design System Component Brief
description: Complete component specs that engineers can build from directly. Output: Component spec in text.
content: Write a component specification for {component_name} in a design system. Include: 1) Component purpose and when to use it (vs. when not to) 2) Props/variants table with type, default, and description 3) Accessibility requirements (ARIA, keyboard, contrast) 4) States: default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, error 5) Usage examples (correct and incorrect side-by-side). Audience: frontend engineers and designers.

title: Literature Review Synthesizer
description: Turn a stack of papers into a structured literature review. Output: Literature review in text.
content: You are a research scholar. Synthesize the following set of papers on {topic}. Produce: 1) A 200-word executive summary of the field consensus 2) Three major themes across the papers with supporting citations 3) The key disagreements or open questions 4) Methodological strengths and gaps 5) Three directions for future research. Papers: {paper_abstracts}

title: Socratic Tutor
description: Learn anything deeply by being guided to discover it yourself. Output: Socratic dialogue in text.
content: Act as a Socratic tutor teaching {concept} to a {level} student. Do not explain the concept directly. Instead: 1) Ask a question that surfaces what they already know 2) Listen for misconceptions in their answer 3) Ask a follow-up that challenges the misconception 4) Guide them to derive the insight themselves 5) Consolidate with a question that tests transfer. If they are stuck, provide the smallest possible hint. Start with your first Socratic question.

title: Rewrite This Simply
description: Turn any complex text into plain, easy-to-read language. Output: Simplified rewrite in text.
content: Take the following text and rewrite it so a 12-year-old could understand it. Keep all the important information but use everyday words, short sentences, and a friendly tone. Remove jargon completely. Text: {text}

title: Write a Thank You Note
description: A genuine thank you note that actually sounds like you. Output: Thank you note in text.
content: Write a heartfelt thank you note to {recipient} for {reason}. Make it feel genuine and personal, not generic. Include a specific detail about why their help/gift/action meant something. Keep it to 3-4 sentences. Tone: {warm/professional/casual}.

title: Turn Bullet Points Into an Email
description: Instantly turn rough notes into a polished email. Output: Full email in text.
content: Turn these bullet points into a clear, professional email. Use a friendly but direct tone. Write a subject line, greeting, body, and sign-off. My name is {name}. Bullet points: {bullets}

title: Write a Caption for This Photo
description: Five ready-to-post Instagram captions for any photo. Output: 5 captions in text.
content: Write 5 different Instagram captions for a photo of {description}. Include: 1) A funny one 2) A heartfelt one 3) A short punchy one (under 8 words) 4) One that asks a question to boost engagement 5) One that tells a mini story. Include 3-5 relevant hashtags for each.

title: Write a Product Description
description: A clear, honest product description that actually sells. Output: Product copy in text.
content: Write a compelling product description for {product_name}. It is used for {purpose} by {target_customer}. Highlight: the main benefit (not just the feature), who it is perfect for, and why it is better than doing nothing. Keep it under 80 words. No hyperbole or buzzwords.

title: Create a Week of Social Posts
description: A full week of social content planned in minutes. Output: 7 ready-to-post captions in text.
content: Create 7 social media posts for a {type_of_business} targeting {audience}. Each post should have: a hook (first line that stops scrolling), the main content (2-3 sentences), and a call to action. Vary the content types: tips, behind-the-scenes, customer story, question, announcement, fun fact, and personal story.

title: Prepare for a Difficult Conversation
description: Go into hard conversations with a clear plan. Output: Conversation prep guide in text.
content: Help me prepare for a difficult conversation with {person} about {topic}. Give me: 1) How to open the conversation without putting them on the defensive 2) Three key points to make clearly 3) How to handle it if they get upset 4) What a good outcome looks like. My goal is: {goal}.

title: Write a Simple Business Plan Summary
description: A clear one-pager that explains your business idea to anyone. Output: One-page plan in text.
content: Write a one-page business plan summary for {business idea}. Include: What it is (1 sentence), Who it is for, The problem it solves, How it makes money, What makes it different, and What is needed to get started. Write it clearly enough that anyone could understand it.

title: Make a Study Plan
description: A realistic, week-by-week plan to learn anything. Output: Study schedule in text.
content: Create a practical study plan for learning {subject} in {timeframe}. I am a {beginner/intermediate} level. Break it into weekly goals, recommend free resources for each week, and include how to test my progress. Make it realistic for someone with {hours_per_week} hours per week.

title: Quiz Me on This Topic
description: Test your understanding of any topic instantly. Output: Quiz questions + answers in text.
content: Create a 10-question quiz on {topic} for someone at the {beginner/intermediate/advanced} level. For each question: write the question, give 4 multiple choice options (labeled A-D), and provide the answer with a brief explanation of why it is correct. Make the questions progressively harder.

title: Explain This Code to Me
description: Understand any code without being a programmer. Output: Plain-English explanation in text.
content: Explain what this code does in plain English. Assume I am not a programmer. Walk through it step by step, explain what each part does, and tell me what the end result is. If there are any potential problems, flag them simply. Code: {code}

title: Write a README for My Project
description: A README that actually gets people excited to use your project. Output: Markdown README file.
content: Write a clear, friendly README for my project called {project_name}. It does: {what_it_does}. Built with: {tech_stack}. Include: a one-sentence description, how to install it, how to use it (with an example), and how someone could contribute. Keep it simple and welcoming for beginners.

title: Give Me Honest Feedback on My Design
description: Honest design critique focused on what actually matters. Output: Design critique in text.
content: Review my design for {what_it_is} and give me honest, actionable feedback. Look at: 1) Is the most important thing the most visually prominent? 2) Is it clear what to do next? 3) Does the spacing feel comfortable or cramped? 4) What is the single biggest thing to fix first? Be direct. I can handle critical feedback.

title: Pick Colors for My Brand
description: A thoughtful color palette picked for your specific brand. Output: Color palette + rationale in text.
content: Help me choose a color palette for {type_of_brand} that targets {audience} and wants to feel {adjective_1} and {adjective_2}. Give me: a primary color (with hex code), a secondary color, an accent color, and a background color. Explain in one sentence why each color fits the brand. Then show an example of how they would work together.

title: Summarize This Article
description: Get the key points from any article in 30 seconds. Output: Summary bullet points in text.
content: Summarize the following article in 5 bullet points. Each bullet should be one clear sentence. Start with the most important point. At the end, add one sentence on what this means practically for someone who {describe_reader}. Article: {article_text}

title: Help Me Decide Between Two Options
description: A clear framework to make any decision with confidence. Output: Decision framework in text.
content: Help me decide between {option_a} and {option_b}. My situation: {context}. What matters most to me: {priorities}. Give me: a quick pros and cons for each (max 3 each), which one you would recommend and why, and the one question I should ask myself before deciding.

title: DCF Valuation Assistant
description: Step-by-step DCF analysis with scenario sensitivity tables. Output: Excel-ready financial model.

title: Stock Earnings Call Summarizer
description: Pull actionable insights from earnings calls in seconds. Output: Structured summary in text.
content:
Summarize the following earnings call transcript. Extract: (1) key financial metrics vs. expectations, (2) management guidance for next quarter, (3) major risks mentioned, (4) analyst Q&A highlights, and (5) an overall sentiment score (bullish/neutral/bearish) with reasoning.

Transcript: {transcript}

title: Personal Budget Optimizer
description: Get a personalized budget analysis and savings plan. Output: Monthly budget plan in text.

title: Tax Deduction Finder
description: Find hidden deductions for your specific situation. Output: Itemized deduction list in text.
content:
I am a {occupation} in {state}. Identify every potentially overlooked tax deduction I might qualify for. For each deduction explain eligibility requirements, estimated value, and documentation needed.

My situation: {situation_details}

title: Crypto Portfolio Risk Analyzer
description: Comprehensive crypto portfolio risk assessment. Output: Risk analysis report in text.

title: Rental Property ROI Analyzer
description: Quick ROI model for any rental property. Output: ROI calculation in text.

title: NDA Clause Red Flag Finder
description: Identify risky NDA clauses before you sign. Output: Annotated clause list in text.
content:
You are a business attorney. Review the NDA below and flag: (1) unusually broad confidentiality provisions, (2) ambiguous definitions, (3) missing standard protections, (4) negotiation recommendations for each issue.

NDA text: {nda_text}

title: Employment Contract Reviewer
description: Understand your employment contract before signing. Output: Plain-English review in text.
content:
Review this employment contract and provide a plain-language summary of: (1) compensation and equity terms, (2) non-compete and non-solicit clauses, (3) IP assignment provisions, (4) termination conditions, (5) red flags for a {role} in {location}.

Contract: {contract_text}

title: Privacy Policy Generator
description: Generate a compliant privacy policy for your business. Output: Full privacy policy document.

title: IP License Term Sheet Drafter
description: Structure an IP licensing deal with a clear term sheet. Output: Term sheet draft in text.

title: Lease Red Flag Finder
description: Find risky lease clauses before you sign. Output: Annotated risk list in text.
content:
Review this lease and identify: (1) unusual tenant-unfavorable clauses, (2) missing standard protections, (3) auto-renewal traps, (4) liability risks, (5) negotiation priorities.

Lease text: {lease_text}

title: Case Brief Generator
description: Generate a complete case brief from any court opinion. Output: Formatted case brief in text.

title: App Concept Validator
description: Stress-test your app idea before you build anything. Output: Validation report in text.
content: I want to build [describe your app idea in 2-3 sentences]. Help me validate this concept by: (1) Identifying the core problem it solves and whether people actually have this problem, (2) Describing the ideal target user in detail, (3) Listing 3 to 5 existing alternatives and how they fall short, (4) Flagging the top 3 risks or assumptions I need to test first, (5) Suggesting a minimum version I could build in 30 days to test the idea. Be direct about weaknesses — do not soften the critique.

title: Technical Roadmap Planner
description: Turn goals into a realistic, prioritized engineering roadmap. Output: Roadmap document in text.
content: I am building [describe your product]. My team has [number] engineers and [number] months before we need to show meaningful results. Here is what we want to achieve: [list your goals]. Create a realistic roadmap that prioritizes ruthlessly based on user impact, identifies dependencies and risks, suggests what to defer or cut, and breaks work into two-week sprints. Flag anything that sounds over-engineered for our stage.

title: AI Workflow Designer
description: Replace repetitive work with a practical, well-designed AI workflow. Output: Workflow design spec in text.
content: I run [describe your business or team role]. My most time-consuming repeated task is: [describe the task in detail]. Design an AI-assisted workflow that: (1) Maps each step of the current process, (2) Identifies which steps AI can handle fully, partially, or not at all, (3) Proposes a new workflow with clear human-to-AI handoffs, (4) Estimates time savings per week, (5) Lists the tools best suited for each step. Write this for someone who is not deeply technical.

title: Security Audit Checklist
description: A launch-ready security checklist any founder can share with their team. Output: Security checklist in text.
content: I am preparing to launch [describe your product or service] and want a thorough security review before going live. Create a comprehensive checklist covering: data storage and encryption, user authentication and access control, third-party integrations, common attack surfaces, and regulatory compliance (GDPR or SOC 2 where relevant). Write this for a non-technical founder who will share it with an engineering team. Include the questions to ask and red flags to watch for.

title: System Architecture Explainer
description: Translate complex technical architecture into language any stakeholder can follow. Output: Architecture explainer in text.
content: I need to explain the technical architecture of [describe your system or product] to [describe your audience: investors, board, new team members, or non-technical stakeholders]. Write a clear, jargon-free explanation that covers: what the system does and why it is built the way it is, how the main components connect, how data flows through the system, how we handle reliability and scale, and what makes our approach defensible. Avoid technical abbreviations without explanation.

title: Vendor Evaluation Framework
description: Choose the right tool with a structured, honest comparison framework. Output: Evaluation scorecard in text.
content: I need to choose between [list 2 to 4 tools, platforms, or vendors] for [describe your use case]. My organization is [small startup, mid-size company, or enterprise] and my main constraints are [budget, time, technical complexity, or compliance requirements]. Build an evaluation framework that: lists the criteria that matter most for my situation, scores each option against those criteria, highlights hidden costs or lock-in risks, and gives a clear recommendation with reasoning. Do not hedge — make a definitive call.

title: Cover Letter That Gets Interviews
description: A cover letter that earns attention in the first sentence. Output: Cover letter in text.
content: I am applying for [job title] at [company name]. Here is what I know about the role: [paste job description or key requirements]. Here is my background: [list your relevant experience in 3 to 5 bullet points]. Write a compelling cover letter that: opens with a specific hook rather than "I am writing to apply," connects my experience directly to their stated needs, shows genuine knowledge of the company, and closes with a confident call to action. Keep it under 350 words. Make it sound human, not templated.

title: Personal Essay That Shows, Not Tells
description: Open your essay with a scene that makes readers stop and lean in. Output: Essay opening in text.
content: I am writing a personal essay about [topic or experience] for [college application, fellowship, or publication]. The main thing I want the reader to understand about me is: [one sentence]. The specific moment or scene I want to open with is: [describe briefly]. Help me write an opening three paragraphs that use sensory detail, resist over-explaining, and create a strong sense of voice. Then give me three suggestions for how the essay could develop from there.

title: Thought Leadership Article Outline
description: Turn your expertise into a publishable article with a clear argument. Output: Article outline in text.
content: I want to write an article about [your topic or thesis] for [target audience: executives, founders, practitioners, or general readers]. My core argument is: [one sentence]. Supporting evidence I have: [list 3 to 5 data points, examples, or observations]. Write a full article outline with: a magnetic headline, a compelling opening paragraph, 4 to 5 sections with subheadings and the key point for each, and a strong conclusion with a clear takeaway. Then write the opening section in full.

title: Academic Essay Polisher
description: Get a rigorous, precise edit on your academic draft. Output: Edited essay in text.
content: Here is a draft of my essay or section: [paste your text]. The essay is for [course, journal, or conference] and the argument I am making is: [one sentence]. Please review this draft and: (1) Identify where the argument is unclear or unsupported, (2) Suggest stronger transitions between paragraphs, (3) Flag any passive voice or wordiness, (4) Recommend where I need more evidence or citation, (5) Rewrite the two weakest paragraphs. Preserve my voice but make the writing sharper and the argument tighter.

title: Keynote Speech Builder
description: Build a speech that moves people, not just informs them. Output: Speech outline in text.
content: I am giving a speech at [event or occasion] to an audience of [describe the audience]. The speech should be approximately [number] minutes. My main message is: [one sentence]. I want the audience to leave feeling: [describe the emotion or insight]. Write a full speech structure with: an opening that creates immediate connection, three narrative movements with clear transitions, at least one specific story that illustrates the main idea, and a closing line they will remember. Then write the opening two minutes in full.

title: Ruthless Edit Pass
description: Cut ruthlessly. Keep only what earns its place on the page. Output: Edited version in text.
content: Here is a piece of writing I want you to edit: [paste your text]. Do a ruthless edit pass that: cuts any sentence that does not earn its place, eliminates hedging language and qualifiers, replaces vague words with specific ones, shortens long paragraphs, and makes the opening sentence impossible to ignore. Show me the before and after side by side for the most significant changes. Aim to cut 20 to 30 percent of the word count while making the piece stronger. Be direct — do not apologize for the cuts.

title: Brand Positioning Statement
description: Sharpen your market position into language that actually sticks. Output: Positioning statement in text.
content: I am building [describe your product or service] for [target audience]. Our main competitors are [list 2 to 3 competitors]. What makes us different is [your differentiator, even if rough]. Help me write: (1) A crisp positioning statement in the format "For [audience] who [need], [brand] is the [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative]," (2) Three alternative taglines, (3) The core emotional promise of the brand in one sentence, (4) The one thing we should never say in our marketing. Push back if my differentiator sounds generic — do not let me hide behind vague language.

title: Social Media Content Calendar
description: A four-week social calendar you can actually stick to. Output: 4-week content calendar in text.
content: I run [describe your business] and want to build a consistent social media presence on [platform or platforms]. My audience is [describe them]. I can commit to posting [number] times per week. My content pillars are: [list 2 to 4 themes I could talk about authentically]. Create a four-week content calendar with: post ideas for each week, a mix of educational, entertaining, and promotional content, suggested formats for each post, and full sample captions for five posts. Make the captions sound like a real person, not a brand account.

title: Cold Email Sequence That Converts
description: Three emails that feel personal, not spammy — and actually get replies. Output: 3-email sequence in text.
content: I am reaching out to [describe your ideal customer] to introduce [your product or service]. The main problem I solve for them is: [one sentence]. My credibility or proof includes: [list any results, clients, or backing]. Write a three-email cold outreach sequence. Email 1: a short, specific opener with one value proposition and a soft call to action. Email 2 (3 days later): a different angle or piece of evidence. Email 3 (5 days later): a graceful closing that leaves the door open. Each email should be under 120 words. Do not use subject lines that look like mass outreach.

title: Product Launch Announcement
description: Write a launch announcement that makes people stop and pay attention. Output: Email + social copy in text.
content: I am launching [product name and one-line description] on [date or timeframe]. The audience I am announcing to is [existing customers, email list, press, or social following]. The core benefit for them is: [one sentence]. The most surprising or impressive thing about the product is: [specific detail]. Write: five launch email subject line options, the full launch email body, a social media announcement post, and a one-paragraph press release opening. Prioritize clarity and genuine excitement over marketing-speak.

title: SEO Content Brief
description: Rank higher by writing articles that actually answer what people are searching for. Output: Editorial brief in text.
content: I want to write an article targeting the search intent behind [keyword or topic]. My website covers [describe your site and audience]. Create a complete SEO content brief including: the primary keyword and 5 to 8 supporting terms, the likely search intent, a recommended title and meta description, a detailed section-by-section outline with subheadings, the top 3 questions this article must answer, and notes on what the best-ranking articles are likely missing. Then write the introduction in full as a model for the tone.

title: Paid Ad Copy Variations
description: Test-ready ad copy with enough variation to find what actually converts. Output: Ad copy variants in text.
content: I am running paid ads for [product or service] targeting [describe audience] on [platform: Meta, Google, or LinkedIn]. The single outcome I want the ad to drive is: [specific action]. My top three customer pain points are: [list them]. Write: (1) Five headline variations under 30 characters each, (2) Three body copy variations with different emotional angles such as urgency, aspiration, and fear of loss, (3) Three call-to-action options, (4) A recommendation on which combination to test first and why. Note which approach tends to perform best on the platform I named.

title: Executive KPI Dashboard
description: Design a dashboard your leadership team will actually read every week. Output: Dashboard spec in text.
content: I lead [describe your team or company] and need to build an executive dashboard that gives leadership a clear view of performance. Our main business goals are: [list 2 to 3 goals]. The audience for this dashboard is [executives, board, investors, or department heads]. Design a KPI framework that: identifies the 6 to 10 most important metrics, groups them by strategic priority, defines how each metric is calculated and where the data comes from, sets a baseline and target for each, and flags which are leading vs. lagging indicators. Format this as a table I can share with my team.

title: Market Sizing Model
description: Build a credible market size estimate that holds up in an investor meeting. Output: Market sizing model in text.
content: I need to estimate the market size for [describe your product or service] to include in an investor pitch or business plan. My target customer is [describe them in detail]. The geography I am focusing on is [region or country]. Walk me through a market sizing approach that: uses both top-down (TAM, SAM, SOM) and bottom-up methods, identifies the key assumptions and where to find data to validate them, shows the math in a format I can build in a spreadsheet, and gives a realistic serviceable market estimate. Flag which assumptions are most uncertain.

title: Customer Survey That People Complete
description: A short, honest survey that gets responses and surfaces real insights. Output: Survey questions in text.
content: I want to run a customer survey to understand [your research question]. My respondents are [describe your customer segment]. I need to learn: [list 2 to 3 specific things]. Design a survey that: stays under 10 questions, uses clear and unbiased language, mixes question types strategically, avoids leading questions, and ends with a question that surfaces something I did not think to ask. Then write an invitation email that achieves a 30 percent or higher response rate from existing customers.

title: Churn Analysis Framework
description: Stop guessing why customers leave. Build a framework that shows you. Output: Churn analysis framework in text.
content: We are experiencing [describe your churn situation: percentage churning, when in the lifecycle, from which segments]. Our product is [brief description]. I want to understand why customers leave and what to do about it. Build a churn analysis framework that: identifies data signals that predict churn before it happens, segments churned customers into meaningful groups, suggests qualitative research to understand the reasons behind the numbers, and recommends the top 3 interventions to test first. Frame this as a team meeting agenda I can run next week.

title: Data Story for Any Audience
description: Turn a data finding into a story that makes non-technical leaders act. Output: Data story narrative in text.
content: I need to present the following finding to [describe audience: CEO, board, sales team, or marketing] who are not data experts: [describe your finding in plain terms, for example "our activation rate dropped 12 percent this quarter"]. The action I want them to take is: [specific ask]. Write a data narrative that: opens with the so-what rather than the methodology, uses an analogy or concrete example to make the number real, acknowledges uncertainty honestly, and ends with a clear recommendation. Suggest one visualization that would make this finding immediately clear.

title: Competitive Landscape Analysis
description: Map your competitive landscape clearly so you know where you can win. Output: Competitive matrix in text.
content: I am analyzing the competitive landscape for [your industry or market]. My company is [brief description]. I want to understand who the key players are, how they are positioned, where the market is moving, and where the gaps are. Structure a complete competitive analysis covering: direct and indirect competitors, the dimensions to evaluate each player on, market share signals and funding trajectories, emerging threats, and a clear view of where we can win. Then apply the framework to [name 3 specific competitors] based on what you know.

title: Brand Identity Brief
description: Give any designer everything they need to get your brand right the first time. Output: Brand identity brief in text.
content: I am building a brand for [describe your company, product, or personal brand]. Our audience is [describe them]. The feeling we want to evoke is [list 3 adjectives]. Our closest competitors look like [describe their aesthetic]. Create a comprehensive brand identity brief covering: brand personality and voice, visual direction including color mood, typography style, and imagery approach, moodboard references to pull from, things our brand should never look like, and three distinct visual directions we could explore. Format this as a brief I can hand directly to a designer.

title: UX Critique and Recommendations
description: Get a structured, expert-level UX critique of any screen or product flow. Output: UX critique report in text.
content: Act as a senior UX designer critiquing [describe the screen, flow, or product you want reviewed]. The primary user goal is: [one sentence]. The main action I want users to take is: [one sentence]. Give me: (1) A structured assessment of what is working and why, (2) The top 5 usability issues ranked by severity, (3) Specific recommendations for each issue, (4) One quick win I can ship this week, (5) One structural change that would meaningfully improve the experience. Be precise — reference layout, hierarchy, copy, and interaction patterns specifically.

title: Presentation Narrative Designer
description: Turn your evidence into a presentation arc that people remember. Output: Slide narrative in text.
content: I need to present [topic] to [audience] in [time available]. The one thing I need them to believe by the end is: [your core message]. Supporting evidence I have: [list your key points or data]. Design the full narrative structure: (1) The opening hook that earns their attention in 60 seconds, (2) The story arc or problem-solution structure, (3) How to sequence my evidence for maximum impact, (4) The closing moment that makes the message stick. Then write the speaker notes for the first slide in full. Design for speaking, not for reading from a screen.

title: Typography and Color System
description: Build a visual language that is coherent, distinctive, and defensible. Output: Typography and color system in text.
content: I am building a visual identity for [describe the brand or project]. The brand personality is [list 3 adjectives]. The primary use case is [digital, print, or both]. The audience is [describe them in detail]. Recommend: (1) A primary typeface pairing with reasoning for each choice, (2) A color palette of 5 to 7 colors with usage rules for each, (3) Spacing and sizing principles, (4) What to avoid for this brand, (5) Examples of brands that use a similar visual language and what we can learn from them. Explain the reasoning behind every choice — not just what, but why.

title: Photography Art Direction Brief
description: Brief any photographer or creative team with confidence and precision. Output: Art direction brief in text.
content: I need to art direct a photo shoot for [describe the product, brand, or campaign]. The mood I am going for is [describe in words or reference brands]. The shots I need are: [list the required deliverables]. The budget is [small, medium, or professional]. Create a complete art direction brief including: mood and feeling guidance, lighting style, color palette and props direction, talent or model direction if applicable, a prioritized shot list, and a section on what to avoid so the photographer knows the boundaries clearly.

title: Design System Component Spec
description: Write a precise component spec that eliminates design-development back-and-forth. Output: Component spec in text.
content: I am building a design system for [describe your product]. The primary platform is [web, mobile, or both]. I need to define the specification for [name the component: button, card, form, modal, or navigation bar]. Write a complete component specification covering: all states including default, hover, active, disabled, loading, and error, accessibility requirements for contrast and screen readers, spacing and sizing variants, usage guidelines for when to use this vs alternatives, and the most common mistake designers make with this component. Format this for a handoff document.

title: User Interview Discussion Guide
description: Run interviews that uncover what people actually think, not what they think you want to hear. Output: Discussion guide in text.
content: I am conducting research on [topic or product area]. The core question I am trying to answer is: [one sentence]. My interview subjects are [describe who they are]. I have approximately [number] minutes per interview. Create a discussion guide that: opens with rapport-building questions, progresses to the core research territory naturally, includes probing follow-ups for the most important questions, avoids leading the participant, and closes with a question that often surfaces surprises. Include facilitator notes on what to listen for and when to dig deeper.

title: Trend Signal Report
description: Distinguish real signals from noise to stay ahead of what matters. Output: Trend signal report in text.
content: I want to identify emerging trends in [industry or topic area] that will matter over the next 2 to 3 years. My role is [describe your context: investor, strategist, product leader, or researcher]. Build a trend analysis covering: (1) 5 to 7 weak signals that are gaining momentum, (2) For each signal: the underlying driver, early evidence, and timeline to mainstream adoption, (3) How these signals might intersect or amplify each other, (4) Which signals represent the biggest opportunities vs. risks for [describe your organization]. Be clear about the difference between hype and durable structural change.

title: Research Proposal Writer
description: Write a research proposal that earns attention and funding. Output: Research proposal in text.
content: I am writing a research proposal for [audience: grant committee, academic supervisor, or company leadership] on the topic of [your research topic]. My central research question is: [one sentence]. My preliminary hypothesis is: [one sentence]. Write a complete proposal including: a compelling statement of the problem and why it matters now, a review of what is already known and the gap that remains, a proposed methodology with rationale, an expected timeline and resource requirements, and anticipated contributions to the field. Keep the language precise and accessible to a non-specialist reader.

title: Competitive Intelligence Brief
description: Build a complete picture of any competitor from publicly available information. Output: Intelligence brief in text.
content: I need to build a competitive intelligence picture on [company or product name]. My context is: [investor due diligence, strategic planning, product development, or sales preparation]. Structure a comprehensive brief covering: business model and revenue streams, product strengths and documented weaknesses, recent strategic moves and what they signal, talent and culture signals from public sources, customer sentiment themes, and where they are likely heading in the next 12 months. Flag what is knowable from public sources vs. what requires primary research. Conclude with the 3 things I should monitor on an ongoing basis.

title: Academic Argument Builder
description: Sharpen your academic argument until it is precise, defensible, and compelling. Output: Argument structure in text.
content: I am writing a paper on [your topic] for [course, journal, or conference]. My central argument is: [your thesis in one sentence]. The strongest counterargument against my position is: [describe it]. Help me: (1) Sharpen my thesis so it is specific and contestable, (2) Structure the argument into 4 to 5 logical steps, (3) Anticipate and address the top 3 objections, (4) Identify what evidence would most strengthen my case, (5) Write a concluding paragraph that synthesizes the argument without simply summarizing it. Point out any logical gaps or assumptions I am relying on.

title: One-Page Business Plan
description: Distill any business idea into a one-pager that earns a real conversation. Output: One-page business plan in text.
content: I want to create a one-page business plan for [describe your idea or company]. Structure it around these sections and fill in what you can from my context, flagging what I need to complete: (1) Problem — what pain exists and who feels it acutely, (2) Solution — what we offer and how it works, (3) Market — how large the opportunity is, (4) Business model — how we make money, (5) Traction — what we have proven so far, (6) Team — why we are the right people for this, (7) Ask — what we need and what we will do with it. Make it tight enough to fit one page and compelling enough to earn a follow-up meeting.

title: Investor Pitch Narrative
description: Build the story behind your pitch — the part that makes investors lean forward. Output: Pitch narrative + 3 slide outlines in text.
content: I am raising [amount] for [describe your company]. We have [describe traction: customers, revenue, or growth]. The problem we solve is: [one sentence]. Our solution is: [one sentence]. Write the narrative arc for my investor pitch that: opens with a memorable statement of the problem, builds the case for why now is the right moment, explains our insight or unfair advantage, shows our path to market leadership, and closes with a vision that makes investors want to be part of it. Also write the three slides investors remember most: problem, solution, and ask.

title: Performance Review Framework
description: Run performance conversations that are honest, kind, and actually useful. Output: Review framework + example in text.
content: I am a manager preparing reviews for my team of [number] people in [department]. I want reviews that are fair, specific, growth-oriented, and lead to real development conversations. Build a performance review framework that: covers the dimensions that matter most for our type of work, uses behavioral anchors rather than vague ratings, includes a structured format for the conversation itself, gives language for delivering both positive and difficult feedback, and ends with a 90-day development plan. Include an example review for a team member who is strong overall but needs to grow in one specific area.

title: Sales Discovery Call Script
description: Ask the questions that open up a real conversation — not a pitch. Output: Discovery call script in text.
content: I am preparing for discovery calls with [describe your ideal customer]. Our product or service is [brief description] and it solves [the main problem]. Before a call, I typically know [what you know about the prospect]. Write a discovery call framework that: builds rapport naturally in the first two minutes, surfaces the real problem with layered questioning, uncovers budget and timeline without being transactional, handles the 3 most common objections for our type of product, and closes the call with a next step both parties are genuinely committed to. Include sample language for each stage.

title: Operational Efficiency Audit
description: Find where your organization is leaking time and money — and fix it systematically. Output: Audit report in text.
content: I run [describe your team or company] and want to identify where we are losing time, money, or quality in our operations. Our main operational activities are: [list 4 to 6 things your team does regularly]. Build an audit framework that: maps each activity against the value it creates, identifies the most common sources of waste or delay, flags which processes depend heavily on a single person, recommends the highest-impact areas to systematize or automate, and suggests a 90-day improvement roadmap. Structure this as a workshop I can run with my leadership team in two hours.

title: Go-to-Market Strategy
description: Choose your first market, your first channel, and your first message — with confidence. Output: Go-to-market plan in text.
content: I am launching [product or service] in [market or geography]. My ideal first customer is [describe them precisely — role, company size, pain level]. My advantage in reaching them is [describe it honestly: channel access, relationships, or domain expertise]. Competitors they currently use include [list them]. Write a go-to-market strategy covering: the beachhead segment and why to start there, the primary channel and the first tactic to use in that channel, the messaging that will resonate at this stage, success metrics for the first 90 days, and the signal that tells us it is time to expand to the next segment.

title: Lesson Plan Builder
description: Design a lesson with a clear arc, a real hook, and a meaningful closing. Output: Lesson plan in text.
content: I am teaching [subject] to [age group or level] and want to create a lesson on [specific topic]. The learning objective is: by the end of this lesson, students will be able to [one clear, measurable outcome]. I have [time available] and the class size is [number of students]. Design a complete lesson plan that: opens with a hook that makes students curious, builds understanding progressively with a clear instructional sequence, includes at least one active learning activity, addresses different learning styles, and closes with a formative check. Include estimated timing for each segment and a materials list.

title: Student Feedback That Motivates Growth
description: Write feedback that students actually read — and act on. Output: Student feedback in text.
content: I am writing feedback on [describe the assignment: essay, project, or presentation] for a student who is [describe their level: struggling, developing, or high-achieving]. The main strength in their work is: [one sentence]. The area most in need of development is: [one sentence]. Write feedback that: opens by anchoring on specific evidence of what worked, identifies the growth area with precise and kind language, gives a concrete strategy they can apply next time, and ends with a statement that builds confidence and agency. Avoid vague praise. Make the student feel seen and capable.

title: Course Learning Journey Map
description: Map a course that takes learners somewhere real — not just through a syllabus. Output: Course learning map in text.
content: I am designing a course on [topic] for [audience: college students, working professionals, or self-learners]. The course runs [duration]. The main transformation I want learners to experience is: [describe where they start and where they finish]. Design a learning journey map that: chunks the content into meaningful modules with clear objectives for each, sequences topics so confidence builds before complexity, identifies where learners typically struggle, suggests varied activity types across modules, and creates a capstone that demonstrates the full learning. Format this so I can share it with co-instructors or a curriculum committee.

title: Parent Update That Gets Read
description: Write parent communications that are clear, warm, and actually get read. Output: Parent letter in text.
content: I need to write a communication to parents about [topic: student progress, upcoming event, classroom change, or behavioral concern]. The key information I need to convey is: [list your main points]. Write a parent communication that: gets to the point in the first two sentences, uses warm and direct language, makes any required action completely clear, anticipates the top concern a parent might have and addresses it proactively, and invites dialogue without creating unnecessary alarm. Keep it under 200 words. Also suggest a subject line that gets the email opened.

title: Socratic Discussion Facilitator
description: Facilitate discussions where students do the thinking — not just the talking. Output: Discussion facilitation guide in text.
content: I am facilitating a discussion on [topic or text] with [age group or level]. The central question I want to explore is: [your question]. Students often avoid or struggle with: [describe a common misconception or resistance pattern]. Design a Socratic discussion that: opens with a low-stakes question everyone can answer, progresses through questions that build complexity and surface genuine disagreement, includes facilitator moves for when discussion goes quiet or loses focus, and closes with a question that lingers after class ends. Include three follow-up probes for the most important questions in the sequence.

title: Teacher Coaching Conversation
description: Have the coaching conversation that actually shifts practice. Output: Coaching conversation guide in text.
content: I am a coach or department head preparing for a professional development conversation with a teacher who [describe the situation: is strong but plateauing, struggling with a specific challenge, or wants to develop a skill]. My goal for this conversation is: [one sentence]. Design a coaching structure that: opens in a way that builds trust and avoids defensiveness, uses inquiry rather than advice-giving, surfaces the teacher's own insight about what is happening, identifies one small experiment they can try before the next conversation, and ends with a clear commitment from both sides. Include sample language I can adapt to my voice.

title: 3-Statement LBO Model Assumptions Audit
description: Senior associate-level review of LBO model assumptions across all three statements. Output: Audit memo in text.
content:
You are a senior investment banking associate reviewing an LBO model. I will share the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement assumptions. For each statement:
1. Flag unrealistic revenue growth rates (benchmark against comparable transactions)
2. Identify margin expansion assumptions that lack operational justification
3. Check working capital assumptions against industry DSO/DIO/DPO norms
4. Verify debt repayment schedule aligns with cash flow availability
5. Test whether exit multiple assumptions are supported by current comp set
Output a structured memo with: (a) critical errors that would kill a deal, (b) aggressive assumptions requiring sensitivity, (c) suggested scenario ranges for each lever. Use the format: [CRITICAL / AGGRESSIVE / ACCEPTABLE] — Finding — Recommendation

title: Monte Carlo Simulation Scenario Brief
description: Structured brief for building a rigorous Monte Carlo simulation on any investment. Output: Simulation design brief in text.
content:
Structure a Monte Carlo simulation brief for the following investment scenario: [describe asset, horizon, and key variables]. For each variable, define:
- Base case assumption and source
- Distribution type (normal, log-normal, triangular, uniform) and justification
- Min / Max / Standard deviation parameters
- Correlation matrix relationships to other variables (if any)
Then specify: number of iterations (justify), key output metrics (IRR, NPV, payback, VaR), and the percentile thresholds that would trigger a pass/fail investment decision. Output as a structured brief a quant analyst could hand directly to a modeler.

title: Debt Covenant Headroom Analysis
description: Calculate covenant headroom, identify trip wires, and draft lender risk language. Output: Analysis memo in text.
content:
I have the following credit agreement covenants: [paste covenant list]. My current financial metrics are: [paste LTM financials]. Walk me through:
1. Calculate current headroom on each financial covenant (leverage, coverage, liquidity)
2. Identify which covenants tighten as EBITDA moves ±10% and ±25%
3. Flag covenant definitions that differ from standard GAAP (addbacks, exclusions, cure rights)
4. Identify the "trip wire" — the first covenant likely to be breached under a stress scenario
5. Draft the key risk disclosure language a lender would require
Present as a covenant compliance matrix with current headroom, stress headroom, and the narrative risk summary.

title: REIT FFO Bridge Analysis
description: NAREIT-compliant FFO/AFFO reconciliation, bridge analysis, and peer benchmarking. Output: Reconciliation tables in text.
content:
I own or am analyzing a REIT. Given the following income statement: [paste]. Help me:
1. Reconcile GAAP net income to FFO (add back depreciation, exclude gains/losses on asset sales per NAREIT definition)
2. Calculate AFFO by further adjusting for recurring capex, straight-line rent normalization, and non-cash compensation
3. Build a bridge from prior period FFO to current period FFO identifying each driver (organic NOI growth, acquisitions, dispositions, financing cost changes)
4. Benchmark the FFO/share growth and AFFO payout ratio against sector peers
5. Flag any non-standard addbacks management is using that a sophisticated analyst would challenge
Output: FFO bridge table, AFFO calculation, and a brief on any accounting red flags.

title: Wash-Sale Rule Exposure Checker
description: Identify wash-sale violations in trading history and quantify disallowed loss exposure. Output: Compliance checklist in text.
content:
Review the following trading history: [paste trades with dates and tickers]. For each realized loss:
1. Identify any substantially identical security purchased within the 61-day window (30 days before + 30 days after the sale)
2. Flag ETFs or funds that may constitute substantially identical securities to individual holdings
3. Calculate the disallowed loss amount and the adjusted cost basis of the replacement security
4. Identify any year-end harvest trades that may inadvertently trigger wash-sale through automatic dividend reinvestment
5. Recommend restructuring trades (e.g., switching to a correlated-but-not-substantially-identical ETF) to preserve tax losses
Output: a wash-sale exposure summary table and the estimated tax impact at [client's marginal rate].

title: Options Greeks Sensitivity Deck
description: Greeks analysis, sensitivity stress-tests, and hedge suggestions for an options book. Output: Analysis brief in text.
content:
I hold the following options positions: [paste positions with strike, expiry, underlying]. For each position and the overall book:
1. Calculate current delta, gamma, theta, vega, and rho (or confirm from provided data)
2. Explain in plain English what each Greek means for MY specific position (not generic)
3. Show how the greeks shift if the underlying moves ±5% and ±15%
4. Identify the "danger zones": price levels and time-decay points where the position is most vulnerable
5. Suggest a hedge for the dominant risk (delta, gamma, or vega) using a position in the same underlying
Format as a position-level Greeks table followed by a plain-language risk narrative a non-quant portfolio manager could act on.

title: MAC Clause Negotiation Redline
description: Red-line analysis of MAC clauses against Delaware precedent and current market standard. Output: Annotated redline in text.
content:
You are M&A counsel reviewing a Material Adverse Change clause in a public company acquisition agreement. Given the following MAC definition: [paste clause]. Perform a red-line analysis:
1. Identify buyer-favorable language that over-broadens the MAC definition (e.g., vague "prospects" inclusion, broad industry carve-out exclusions)
2. Identify seller-favorable language that may prevent the buyer from walking even in severe deterioration scenarios
3. Flag any post-COVID litigation risk based on Delaware court precedent (AB Stable VIII, Akorn)
4. Propose specific redline language for: (a) pandemic/epidemic carve-out scope, (b) disproportionate impact test, (c) buyer-knowledge carve-out
5. Assess overall clause as buyer-friendly, seller-friendly, or balanced against current market standard
Output as: current language → proposed language → rationale, followed by an overall MAC risk rating.

title: IP Chain-of-Title Audit
description: Trace IP ownership, identify chain-of-title gaps, and produce a remediation checklist. Output: Audit checklist in text.
content:
I am acquiring a company or licensing IP. Review the following documents: [paste employment agreements, consulting agreements, assignment agreements, patent assignments]. For each piece of IP:
1. Trace chain of title from creator → employer/assignee → current owner
2. Identify gaps: inventors not employed at time of invention, consultants without valid IP assignment clauses, joint ownership situations
3. Flag jurisdictions where moral rights or shop rights may cloud title
4. Identify any third-party licenses, encumbrances, or government funding (Bayh-Dole Act implications) that limit the IP's commercialization
5. Draft a chain-of-title remediation checklist: what assignments, confirmations, or waivers are needed before closing
Output as an IP risk matrix: asset → risk level → remediation required → priority.

title: GDPR Article 30 Record of Processing Activities
description: Build a GDPR-compliant Article 30 ROPA with legal basis analysis and DPIA flags. Output: ROPA document in text.
content:
Help me build a compliant Article 30 ROPA for the following business unit: [describe business unit, data flows, systems used]. For each processing activity identified:
1. Document: controller/processor name, DPO contact, purpose of processing, legal basis, categories of data subjects, categories of personal data, recipient categories, third-country transfers (with safeguard mechanism), retention period, and technical/organizational security measures
2. Identify processing activities that lack a documented legal basis and recommend the most defensible basis (consent, legitimate interest, contract, legal obligation)
3. Flag processing activities that likely require a DPIA (large-scale, systematic monitoring, sensitive data)
4. Identify any third-country transfers lacking adequate safeguards post-Schrems II
Output as a structured ROPA table in Article 30 format, followed by a risk priority list.

title: Force Majeure Applicability Analysis
description: Clause-by-clause force majeure applicability analysis with jurisdiction-specific case law. Output: Legal analysis memo in text.
content:
Given this force majeure clause: [paste clause] and this dispute: [describe event and performance failure], analyze:
1. Does the triggering event fall within the clause's enumerated categories or general catch-all? Cite textual arguments for both sides.
2. Assess the "beyond reasonable control" standard — what steps would a court expect the affected party to have taken?
3. Evaluate the notice requirement: was notice given in the required form, to the right party, within the required timeframe?
4. Analyze the mitigation obligation: what alternative performance was available and not pursued?
5. Research applicable governing law (specify jurisdiction): how have courts in this jurisdiction interpreted similar clauses, particularly post-COVID?
6. Provide a probability assessment: strong FM defense, weak FM defense, or borderline — with key swing factors.
Output as a structured legal memorandum.

title: Non-Solicitation Enforceability Opinion
description: Enforceability opinion on non-solicitation agreements with jurisdiction-specific analysis. Output: Legal opinion in text.
content:
Review this non-solicitation agreement: [paste agreement]. Analyze enforceability under the following frameworks:
1. Geographic and temporal scope: is the restriction reasonable in duration and geography given the employee's role and access to confidential information?
2. Protectable interest: does the employer have a legitimate protectable interest (customer relationships, trade secrets, specialized training) that justifies the restriction?
3. Blue-penciling: would a court in [specify jurisdiction] reform an overbroad clause or void it entirely?
4. Consideration: was adequate consideration provided at signing (particularly for mid-employment agreements post-Fifield)?
5. Recent legislative/regulatory changes: has the jurisdiction restricted or banned non-competes/non-solicits (FTC rule, state statutes)?
6. Enforcement risk factors: what facts make enforcement more or less likely?
Output: enforceability opinion (strong/moderate/weak/unenforceable) with jurisdiction-specific reasoning.

title: Deposition Outline and Impeachment Map
description: Structured deposition outline with impeachment map, document authentication, and prior-statement traps. Output: Deposition outline in text.
content:
I am preparing for a deposition of [describe witness: role, relationship to case, expected testimony]. Given these case facts: [paste relevant facts and documents]. Build:
1. Chronological outline of examination topics with specific open-ended questions designed to lock in the witness's story
2. Document impeachment map: for each key document [list exhibits], draft the foundational questions to authenticate and the impeachment sequence if the witness denies or contradicts the document
3. Prior statement inconsistency tracker: identify 3–5 statements from prior testimony, declarations, or emails that contradict the witness's likely testimony and draft the impeachment question sequence
4. Adverse inference opportunities: flag areas where the witness may invoke privilege or claim lack of memory and how to build the adverse inference record
5. "Safe harbor" questions: areas where you let the witness testify freely because it helps your case
Output as a structured deposition outline with tabs for direct, impeachment, and safe harbor.

title: Blameless Post-Mortem Facilitator
description: Structured blameless post-mortem with contributing factor analysis and actionable follow-ups. Output: Post-mortem document in text.
content:
We had an incident: [describe what failed, when, duration, customer impact]. Facilitate a blameless post-mortem:
1. Build a precise timeline: from first alert or symptom through detection, diagnosis, mitigation, and resolution — include who did what and when
2. Identify contributing factors at each layer (code, configuration, deployment process, monitoring, on-call process, communication) without attributing blame to individuals
3. For each contributing factor, ask "why did the system allow this?" rather than "who did this?"
4. Distinguish between: immediate cause, contributing causes, and root causes
5. Generate action items using the format: [Prevent / Detect / Mitigate / Process] — specific action — owner — due date — success metric
6. Draft the customer-facing incident summary (honest but measured, appropriate for status page and email)
Output: blameless post-mortem document ready to share with engineering leadership.

title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR)
description: Complete ADR documenting a technical decision with alternatives, tradeoffs, and consequences. Output: ADR document in text.
content:
I need to document an architectural decision: [describe the decision to be made]. Write a complete Architecture Decision Record following this structure:
**Status:** [Proposed / Accepted / Deprecated / Superseded]
**Context:** What is the technical and business situation forcing this decision? What constraints exist (team size, timeline, existing systems, cost)?
**Decision:** State the architectural choice clearly and unambiguously.
**Considered Alternatives:** For each alternative (minimum 3), document: what it is, why it was considered, its key tradeoffs, and why it was rejected.
**Consequences:** Document both positive consequences AND the debt/tradeoffs this decision creates. Be honest about what becomes harder.
**Compliance:** What governance, security, or regulatory requirements does this address or create?
**Review Date:** When should this decision be revisited?
Format as a Markdown document suitable for a Git repository.

title: STRIDE Threat Model
description: STRIDE threat model with DFD mapping, risk scoring, and prioritized remediation backlog. Output: Threat model report in text.
content:
Perform a STRIDE threat model for the following system: [describe system architecture, data flows, trust boundaries, actors]. For each component and data flow:
1. Map the system as a Data Flow Diagram: identify processes, data stores, external entities, and trust boundaries
2. For each element, enumerate threats using STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege
3. For each identified threat, assign: likelihood (High/Med/Low), impact (High/Med/Low), and DREAD-style risk score
4. Map each threat to a mitigation control (existing or recommended) and categorize as: [Mitigated / Partially Mitigated / Accepted Risk / Open]
5. Generate a prioritized remediation backlog sorted by risk score
6. Identify the top 3 "crown jewel" attack paths an adversary would most likely target
Output as a structured threat model document with a risk registry table.

title: Product Requirements Document (PRD) One-Pager
description: Tight, opinionated PRD one-pager that gives engineers everything they need and nothing they do not. Output: PRD document in text.
content:
Write a concise PRD one-pager for the following feature: [describe the feature idea and user problem]. Structure it as:
**Problem Statement:** What specific user pain point does this solve? Cite data or research if available.
**Who:** Primary persona (role, key motivation, current workaround)
**Success Metrics:** 3–5 measurable outcomes that define success. Each must have a baseline, target, and timeline.
**Scope:** What is explicitly IN scope for the first release. What is explicitly OUT of scope (and why).
**User Stories:** 5–8 stories in "As a [persona], I want to [action] so that [outcome]" format, prioritized by impact
**Open Questions:** Unresolved decisions that need input before engineering begins, with who owns each
**Dependencies & Risks:** Technical, legal, or resourcing dependencies; top 2–3 risks with mitigation
Keep the entire document under 500 words. Every sentence should help an engineer understand what to build.

title: LLM Evaluation Rubric Builder
description: Task-specific LLM evaluation rubric with behavioral anchors, canary test set, and HITL thresholds. Output: Evaluation rubric in text.
content:
I am evaluating LLM outputs for the following use case: [describe the task, inputs, and what good output looks like]. Build a rigorous evaluation rubric:
1. Define 5–8 evaluation dimensions specific to this task (e.g., factual accuracy, instruction following, format compliance, reasoning transparency, tone appropriateness, hallucination rate)
2. For each dimension: write a precise definition, a 1–5 scoring scale with behavioral anchors at each level, and 1–2 example outputs at the low and high ends
3. Design a "canary set": 10 test inputs that would stress-test each dimension — include edge cases, adversarial inputs, and ambiguous instructions
4. Specify the aggregation method: should dimensions be equally weighted, or should some (e.g., factual accuracy) be gates that override the composite score?
5. Define a human-in-the-loop review threshold: what composite score triggers mandatory human review before output is used?
Output as a complete evaluation rubric document ready to give to a rater team or plug into an auto-eval pipeline.

title: API Contract Design Review
description: Scored API contract review covering naming, status codes, idempotency, versioning, and security. Output: Review report in text.
content:
Review this API design: [paste API specification or describe endpoints]. Evaluate against these criteria:
1. **Naming consistency:** Are resources named with nouns (not verbs)? Are pluralization and casing consistent?
2. **Status code correctness:** Are HTTP status codes semantically correct for each operation's success and error states?
3. **Idempotency:** Are PUT and DELETE operations truly idempotent? Is there a safe retry strategy for POST?
4. **Pagination:** Does the API paginate large collections? Is the pagination strategy (cursor vs. offset) appropriate for the data characteristics?
5. **Versioning strategy:** How will breaking changes be introduced? Is the versioning mechanism (URL path, header, query param) consistent?
6. **Error response schema:** Are errors structured consistently? Do they include a machine-readable code and a human-readable message?
7. **Security:** Are authentication and authorization requirements documented per endpoint? Are sensitive fields excluded from responses?
Output: a scored API review (each criterion 1–5) plus a prioritized list of changes before the API goes to consumers.

title: Long-Read Article Structural Outline
description: Complete structural outline for a long-read article with lede variants, section architecture, and reporting gaps. Output: Article brief in text.
content:
I am writing a long-form piece (2,500–5,000 words) on: [topic]. Target publication: [outlet or audience]. Build a complete structural outline:
1. **Lede:** Write 3 alternative ledes — anecdotal, scene-setting, and data-driven. Flag which is strongest and why.
2. **Nut graf:** Draft the nut graf that tells readers why this story matters right now.
3. **Section architecture:** Name each section (5–8), describe the primary argument or revelation in each, and identify the type of evidence needed (expert quote, data point, case study, document).
4. **Narrative tension arc:** Map where the story builds, where it complicates, and where it resolves.
5. **Kicker:** Draft 2 possible closing lines — one that echoes the lede, one that opens outward.
6. **Reporting gap check:** What 3 questions must be answered before this piece can be published?
Output as a working outline a reporter could hand to an editor for green-light approval.

title: Op-Ed Argument Sharpener
description: Argument stress-test for op-eds — steel-man, load-bearing claims, fresh angle, and thesis variants. Output: Op-ed structure in text.
content:
I want to write an op-ed arguing: [state your core thesis]. Target outlet: [publication]. Help me strengthen this argument:
1. **Steel-man the opposition:** What is the single strongest counterargument to my thesis? How would a smart, good-faith opponent frame it?
2. **Identify the load-bearing claims:** Which 2–3 claims must be true for my thesis to hold? Are these claims supported by evidence, or are they assumptions?
3. **Find the fresh angle:** What do most people already believe about this topic, and how does my argument add something new rather than restating conventional wisdom?
4. **Evidence audit:** For each major claim, classify the evidence as: (a) strong and citable, (b) directionally suggestive but not conclusive, or (c) assumption requiring acknowledgment
5. **Concession strategy:** What can I concede to a reader who disagrees without undermining my core thesis? Concession makes argument more credible.
6. **Draft the thesis sentence:** Write 3 versions — 25 words or fewer — that could open or close the piece.
Output as an argument memo I can use to draft the full piece.

title: Voice and Tone Audit
description: Deep voice and tone audit with rewrite — fingerprints, consistency, audience calibration, and sentence-level fixes. Output: Style audit memo + rewrite in text.
content:
Audit the voice and tone of this writing sample: [paste 300–600 words]. Analyze:
1. **Voice fingerprint:** Identify 5 specific voice characteristics (sentence length patterns, use of first/second/third person, verb strength, formality register, use of hedging language). Quote examples from the text.
2. **Tone consistency:** Does the tone stay consistent throughout, or does it shift? Where does it drift and why?
3. **Audience calibration:** Based on the vocabulary, reference set, and assumed knowledge, who is this written for? Does that match the stated audience?
4. **Show vs. tell ratio:** Identify 3 places where the writer tells the reader something that could be shown more vividly.
5. **Sentence-level issues:** Flag the 3 most common sentence-level problems (passive voice overuse, nominalization, throat-clearing openers, buried verbs).
6. **Rewrite sample:** Choose the weakest paragraph and rewrite it in a stronger version of the same voice.
Output as a style audit memo followed by the rewritten paragraph.

title: Keynote Speech Arc Builder
description: Complete keynote architecture — hook options, one-thing distillation, body structure, pivot, CTA, and closing callback. Output: Speech architecture brief in text.
content:
I am giving a keynote on [topic] to [audience: size, role, context] in [duration] minutes. Build the complete speech architecture:
1. **Opening hook (60 seconds):** Write 3 options — a counterintuitive claim, a story that reframes the topic, and a question the audience has never been asked. Score each on memorability and relevance.
2. **Core idea (the "one thing"):** Distill the speech to a single sentence a listener could repeat at dinner that night. Test it: is it specific? Is it surprising? Is it useful?
3. **Three-part body structure:** For each section, define: the argument, the evidence type (data, story, analogy, demonstration), and the transition to the next section.
4. **The pivot:** Identify the moment in the speech where the tone shifts — where you move from identifying a problem to offering a path forward.
5. **Call to action:** What specific, doable action do you want every person to take in the next 48 hours?
6. **Closing callback:** Draft a closing line that echoes the opening and gives the audience a feeling of completion.
Output as a speech architecture brief with timing estimates for each section.

title: Academic Abstract Polisher
description: Structured abstract polishing — gap check, precision audit, jargon calibration, active voice, and finding prominence. Output: Annotated feedback + clean abstract in text.
content:
Polish this academic abstract: [paste abstract]. Apply these criteria strictly:
1. **Structure check:** Does the abstract include: background/context, research gap or question, methodology, key findings, and implications? Flag any missing element.
2. **Precision audit:** Replace every vague word ("significant," "interesting," "many," "some") with a precise term or quantified claim.
3. **Jargon calibration:** Identify terms that would not be understood by a scholar in an adjacent field. Either simplify or define briefly.
4. **Active voice conversion:** Rewrite any passive constructions that obscure agency ("it was found that" → "we found").
5. **Finding prominence:** Is the most important finding in the first or second sentence? If not, restructure.
6. **Word count discipline:** If over 250 words (or the journal's limit), identify what to cut without losing substance.
Output: annotated original with issues marked, then a clean polished version.

title: ICP Hypothesis Stress-Test
description: ICP hypothesis stress-test — specificity, falsifiability, beachhead vs. TAM, internal validation signals. Output: ICP definition doc in text.
content:
My Ideal Customer Profile is: [describe ICP: company size, industry, role, pain point, buying trigger]. Stress-test this hypothesis:
1. **Specificity check:** Rate each ICP dimension (1–5) for specificity. "Mid-market" is not specific. "Series B SaaS companies with 50–200 employees growing > 30% YoY" is specific. Rewrite any vague dimensions.
2. **Falsifiability test:** What would disprove this ICP? If you can't name 3 things that would cause you to revise it, the ICP is not testable.
3. **Beachhead vs. TAM:** Is this ICP a beachhead (narrow, winnable, expandable) or an aspiration (too broad to own)? Suggest how to narrow if needed.
4. **Internal validation:** What data from your CRM, product analytics, or sales calls would confirm or deny this ICP? List 5 specific signals.
5. **Counter-profile:** Define the anti-ICP — the company type that looks similar but consistently churns or never closes. This is as important as the ICP itself.
6. **Adjacent ICP:** Identify one adjacent ICP that shares the same underlying pain point and could be expanded into after the beachhead is won.
Output as an ICP validation memo with a revised ICP statement.

title: NPS Verbatim Theme Coder
description: Systematic NPS verbatim analysis — theme coding, driver vs. dissatisfier, priority matrix, and competitive signals. Output: Analysis report in text.
content:
I have the following NPS verbatim responses: [paste 20–50 open-text responses with scores]. Analyze them systematically:
1. **Sentiment-score alignment check:** Identify promoters (9–10) with negative verbatims and detractors (0–6) with positive verbatims — these mixed signals are your highest-signal data.
2. **Theme extraction:** Group all verbatims into 5–8 themes. For each theme: name it precisely, quote 2–3 representative verbatims, and calculate what % of responses mention it.
3. **Driver vs. dissatisfier classification:** Classify each theme as a satisfaction driver (present = good, absent = neutral) or a dissatisfier (present = bad, absent = neutral). These require different responses.
4. **Priority matrix:** Map themes by frequency and sentiment impact. Which themes appear often AND drive score negatively? These are your product/service priorities.
5. **Competitive signal scan:** Flag any verbatims that mention a competitor by name or by implication ("before we used X" or "unlike our last vendor").
6. **Recommended actions:** For the top 3 priority themes, draft a specific product, ops, or communication action.
Output as a theme analysis table followed by an executive summary with 3 recommended actions.

title: Email Subject Line Optimization Suite
description: Subject line scoring, rewrite, preview text pairing, and A/B test design for email campaigns. Output: Subject line variants + test plan in text.
content:
I need to optimize email subject lines for this campaign: [describe campaign goal, audience, and 3–5 draft subject lines]. For each draft subject line:
1. **Curiosity gap analysis:** Does the subject line create a gap between what the reader knows and what they want to know? Rate 1–5.
2. **Specificity score:** Vague ("You might like this") performs worse than specific ("3 ways to cut your report time in half"). Score and rewrite any vague subjects.
3. **Personalization opportunity:** Where can a merge field (name, company, behavior trigger) increase relevance without feeling creepy?
4. **Preview text optimization:** Write a complementary preview text (40–90 chars) for each subject line that extends rather than repeats the hook.
5. **Mobile rendering check:** At 40 characters, what does each subject line look like? Rewrite any that get cut off at a bad point.
6. **A/B test design:** Select the 2 strongest candidates and design a statistically valid A/B test: recommended sample size per variant, primary metric, secondary metrics, and minimum detectable effect.
Output: scored subject line table, rewritten versions, preview text pairs, and A/B test spec.

title: Paid Search Quality Score Audit
description: Paid search QS audit — keyword-ad alignment, match type strategy, negative keywords, and landing page fixes. Output: Audit report in text.
content:
Audit the following paid search campaign structure: [paste ad groups, keywords, ad copy, and landing page URL or description]. Evaluate:
1. **Keyword-to-ad relevance:** For each ad group, does the keyword theme appear in the headline, description, and display URL? Flag mismatches that would depress Quality Score.
2. **Match type strategy:** Are broad match keywords creating irrelevant impressions? Are exact match keywords so narrow they limit volume? Recommend the right match type mix.
3. **Negative keyword gaps:** Based on the keyword list, what are 10 obvious negative keywords that are probably driving wasted spend?
4. **Ad copy differentiation:** Does each ad variant test a meaningfully different value proposition, or are variants just word-swaps? Rewrite 2 headlines that test a genuinely different angle.
5. **Landing page alignment:** Does the landing page headline match the ad's promise? Identify 3 landing page changes that would improve conversion rate and Quality Score simultaneously.
6. **Bidding strategy fit:** Given the campaign goal (traffic / leads / ROAS), is the current bidding strategy (manual CPC, tCPA, tROAS, Maximize Clicks) the right fit?
Output as a Quality Score audit checklist with priority fixes ranked by estimated impact.

title: Content Cluster Authority Map
description: Content cluster strategy — pillar definition, cluster mapping, internal linking architecture, and 90-day roadmap. Output: Content strategy map in text.
content:
Build a content cluster strategy for the topic: [describe topic area and target audience]. My domain currently ranks for: [list any known keywords or rankings]. Structure the plan:
